qué compilar y con qué: what to compile and with what
El archivo fuente que exporta tu editor:
The source file your editor exports (J.A.C.K., Hammer). You can also drag it onto the window.

The .bsp, .prt and logs are written next to this file, unless you set an output folder.
La carpeta con sdHLCSG, sdHLBSP, sdHLVIS:
The folder with sdHLCSG, sdHLBSP, sdHLVIS and sdHLRAD. If you built this repo, it's the 'tools' folder. The GUI finds it by itself on startup.

CAREFUL: if you point it at another program's folder (JACK, Hammer, an old install), updating the app does NOT update those binaries. The app only replaces the 'tools' folder next to it. If that happens, you'll get a warning right below.
Estas herramientas son más viejas que la: These tools are older than the ones that come with this version of the app. Updating the app doesn't touch a folder pointing somewhere else, so you'd be compiling with the old binaries and without the new options
Ahora se usan las herramientas de la app: The app's tools are in use now
Dónde queda el .bsp. Si la dejas vacía,:
Where the .bsp ends up. If you leave it empty, the .bsp is written next to the .map (and if 'Folder per project' is on, the compile's leftovers go to an 'intermedios' subfolder right there).

If you set it, the .map is copied there and that copy is compiled: the .bsp, the .prt, the logs and the intermediates (.p0 to .p3) all stay in that folder and your working folder stays clean. The original .map is never touched.
Dónde tienes tus .wad. Sirve para dos co:
Where your .wad files are. It's used for two things:

1) It's passed to RAD as -waddir so it finds the textures when computing the light.
2) If you turn on the option below, the map's WAD list is rewritten to point at this folder.
Con esto activado, la carpeta de salida:
With this on, the output folder doesn't fill up with loose files: a folder named after the project (or the map, if there's no project) is created inside it, and inside that, an 'intermedios' subfolder.

The compile runs in 'intermedios', so EVERYTHING the tools leave behind stays there: the copy of the .map, the logs, the .prt, the .p0 to .p3, the .lin and the .pts. When it ends well, the .bsp alone is moved one level up.

Result: in the project folder you see the .bsp and nothing else. You can point ten maps at the same output folder without them mixing.

It also works without an output folder: no project folder is created (the .bsp still ends up next to the .map, where you expect it), but the 'intermedios' subfolder is, right beside it, so your source folder stays clean.
{folder}\\ para el .bsp, {folder}\\{work: {folder}\ for the .bsp, {folder}\{work}\ for logs and intermediates
Todo suelto en la carpeta de salida: Everything loose in the output folder
Sin carpeta de salida: el .bsp junto al: No output folder: the .bsp next to the .map, {work}\ beside it for logs and intermediates
Todo suelto junto al .map, mezclado con: Everything loose next to the .map, mixed with your sources
Un .map guarda las rutas absolutas de lo:
A .map stores the absolute paths of the WADs on the machine where it was made: 'C:/Users/Someone/...', or worse, paths without a drive letter like '/Users/Admin/...', which Windows resolves against the current drive. If the map came from another PC, another drive, or you simply moved your WADs, CSG dies with 'Could not open wad file'.

With this on, every entry in the list is checked before compiling: the ones that exist are kept, the broken ones are searched by file name in your WAD folder (subfolders included), next to the .map and in the tools folder. sdhlt.wad is always added.

If textures are still missing, the ones the map actually uses are read and the index of every .wad in your folders is opened to see which one has them: only the ones that contribute something are loaded. You can have a thousand WADs in the folder; only the needed ones get in. Capped at 500, leaving room under this fork's limit of 512.

The resulting list is passed to CSG as -wadcfgfile, which makes it ignore the map's key. Your .map is not modified and no output folder is needed. Anything not found is reported in the log instead of killing the compile.
Indica una carpeta de WADs para poder re: Set a WAD folder so the missing ones can be relocated
Las rutas rotas se buscan por nombre en: Broken paths are searched by name in that folder
CSG usará las rutas del .map tal cual: r: CSG will use the .map's paths as they are: risk of 'Could not open wad file'
un punto de partida; después ajusta lo q: a starting point; adjust whatever you like afterwards
Configuración personalizada: no coincide: Custom settings: they don't match any preset exactly.
puedes saltar las que ya ejecutaste: you can skip the ones you already ran
Activa al menos una etapa. Una ejecución: Turn on at least one stage. An empty run produces nothing.
0 = usar todos los núcleos, que es lo qu: 0 = use every core, which is what you want. This fork fixed two bugs that made the tools run on a single thread. Set a number only if you want to leave CPU free for something else.
Corre las herramientas con prioridad baj: Runs the tools at low priority so the PC stays usable while compiling. Makes the compile a little longer.
Al final, cada herramienta imprime cuánt: At the end, every tool prints how much of each engine limit you are using. It's how you find out you're heading for a limit before hitting it. Leave it on.
Las herramientas imprimen mucho más sobr: The tools print much more about what they're doing. Useful when something fails and you don't know why; for normal use it just clutters the log.
recorta brushes y resuelve texturas; cen: clips brushes and resolves textures; hundredths of a second
Copia dentro del .bsp las texturas que e:
Copies into the .bsp the textures the map actually uses (not the whole WAD, only the ones that appear).

WHAT CHANGES: players no longer need the WAD. No more 'missing texture' when joining the server, and no extra files to distribute. In exchange the .bsp grows, typically between a few hundred KB and a few MB depending on how many custom textures you use.

On by default because it's what saves players trouble. Turn it off only if you distribute the WAD yourself and care about the .bsp's size.
Por defecto este fork compila de forma r:
By default this fork compiles reproducibly: the same .map always gives the same .bsp, byte for byte.

WHAT CHANGES: turning this on brings back the original behavior, where two compiles of the same map can differ in a few clipnodes and marksurfaces, because CSG numbers the planes by whichever thread wins the race. Saves ~0.1% of the total time.

Determinism matters when you're chasing a bug: if the map comes out with an odd crack, you want it to come out the same on the next compile instead of vanishing by itself.
Junta en una sola entidad las entidades:
Joins into a single entity the brush entities that are interchangeable with each other. The brushes are not touched: same geometry, same textures, same lighting, same collisions. The only thing that changes is which entity they hang from.

WHAT CHANGES: every brush entity costs a BSP model, and those models come out of the same precache table shared by player, weapon and sprite models. A field of 200 bushes made with func_illusionary goes from using 200 slots to using a few, one per area. That is paid per entity, not per brush: a 1-brush func_illusionary and an 80-brush one cost the same.

FOR YOUR BUSHES TO MERGE, in the editor:
· classname func_illusionary (or func_wall)
· texture with '{' and rendermode Solid, renderamt 255
· NO targetname, no target, no origin brush
· all with exactly the same keyvalues

You do NOT have to group them by hand in the editor. The compiler groups them by proximity on its own, and by hand it's easier to slip something with a name into the group.

It only takes ONE key differing (a different renderamt, zhlt_noclip set on some and not others) for them to go into separate groups. That's not a bug: it's the guarantee that merging doesn't change behavior.

To leave a particular entity out, give it zhlt_nomerge 1.

HOW TO TELL IF IT WORKED: when CSG ends, the log says 'Merged N static brush entities into M'. If it says 0, or doesn't show up, something disqualifies them; turn on 'Verbose' and the log lists every group it did build.

WHEN NOT TO USE IT: if your map has few brush entities you gain nothing. This is for maps with lots of repeated decoration.

See docs/MERGE_DE_ENTIDADES.md.
si usas mucha decoración: if you use lots of decoration
En el editor: func_illusionary + textura: In the editor: func_illusionary + '{' texture + rendermode Solid + renderamt 255, no targetname. They group themselves, don't join them by hand
Hasta cuántas unidades puede medir, en c:
How many units, on any axis, a merged group's box can measure. It's the only value you might want to touch, and only if you know what your map is like.

WHAT CHANGES: a brush entity is culled by its model's bounding box: if the box is not in the player's PVS, it is neither sent nor drawn. If the whole map were merged into one entity, that box would be the size of the map and would be in the PVS from almost anywhere, so decoration you can't see would be drawn. The limit keeps each group within something like a sector.

VALUES:
· 512 — maps of corridors and small rooms, finer culling
· 1024 — the default, fine for almost everything
· 2048 — open maps, where the PVS is poor anyway and saving more slots pays off
· 0 — no limit. Don't use it unless you're running out of models and don't care about performance

If after raising it you see decoration being drawn from far away in r_speeds, lower it.
Sin límite: la caja de un grupo puede ab: No limit: a group's box can span the whole map and always be in the PVS. You save models and lose culling
Grupos grandes: solo para mapas abiertos: Large groups: only for open maps. Check r_speeds before leaving it like this
Déjalo apagado salvo que sepas exactamen:
Leave it off unless you know exactly why you're turning it on.

By default only the render modes the engine does NOT sort by depth are merged: Normal and Solid. Solid is the alpha test of '{' textures — the one foliage uses — and it cuts the pixel instead of blending it, so there's nothing to sort. That's why the bushes case gets in with no restrictions and you don't need this option.

WHAT CHANGES: it adds the modes that do blend (Texture, Additive, Glow, Color). The engine sorts them using a single point per entity; if you merge several into one, they all share that point and can be drawn in the wrong order among themselves. One pane of glass shows in front of another that is actually closer.

It only makes sense if you have many blended entities together in an area where they don't overlap visually. And you have to check it in the game, because the compiler can't warn you about this.
Los cristales y efectos aditivos fusiona: Merged glass and additive effects may draw in the wrong order among themselves. Check it in the game
No cambia el .bsp. Solo añade un informe:
Doesn't change the .bsp. It only adds a report at the end of CSG saying which textures are bloating it.

WHAT FOR: if you compile with 'Embed textures', the texture lump is usually most of the file. Measured on real maps: 82.8% and 69.9% of the .bsp, against 8.7% and 15.4% for the lighting. The normal chart gives you a single total and that's it; this one tells you what it's made of.

WHAT TO LOOK AT, the 'oversampled' column: how many pixels the texture has for every pixel that actually gets shown. It's computed from the real surface it paints in the map and the texture scale, it's not an estimate.
· 4x or more — it has resolution to spare. You can halve it on each axis and still have one pixel per screen pixel
· around 1x — it's used at its native resolution, leave it alone
· below 1x — it repeats over a large surface. Lowering it will show

That column is the reason for the option. Looking only at size, it seems that shrinking every 256px texture would save a ton, and on a real measured map it turned out none had resolution to spare: they were textures repeated over huge walls and shrinking them would only have looked worse.

It also warns if two textures have identical pixels, which is weight paid twice.

WHEN TO USE IT: when the .bsp weighs more than you'd like. No need to leave it on for every compile.
cuando quieras adelgazar el mapa: when you want to slim down the map
Mira la columna 'oversampled': 4x o más: Look at the 'oversampled' column: 4x or more means you can halve that texture without it showing. Around 1x, leave it
Quita las caras del mundo que un func_wa:
Removes the world faces a func_wall covers completely: the engine draws them and RAD lights them even though nobody can see them. It's what you'd do by hand with the NULL texture, without touching the editor.

ONLY func_walls that never change COUNT: no targetname, rendermode Normal, no zhlt_invisible or zhlt_noclip, and all their faces in opaque textures (no '{', water or tool textures). A func_illusionary doesn't count: it isn't solid and a player can get inside and see what it covers.

A face is only removed if a brush of the func_wall covers it entirely, with at least 1 unit of thickness in front. If it only covers part of it, it stays as is.

HOW TO TELL HOW MANY IT REMOVED: the CSG log says '-autonull: N world faces hidden by a func_wall set to NULL'. The Analysis tab lists the ones left.

WHEN NOT TO USE IT: if a server plugin moves, hides or deletes unnamed func_walls, the gap would be in plain sight.
Sube el límite de geometría más allá de: Raises the geometry limit past +/-32768 units. Only if your map really exceeds the standard size; 0 keeps the default value.
vertex manipulation de J.A.C.K. y Hammer: vertex manipulation in J.A.C.K. and Hammer
Cuando mueves vértices en el editor, una:
When you move vertices in the editor, a face can stop being flat: the editor draws it with its vertices, but the compiler only stores 3 points per face and builds the plane from them. The solid that gets compiled is not the one you see, and invisible faces, slits or NULL faces show up in the game.

WHAT CHANGES: CSG detects those brushes and rebuilds them as the convex solid of their vertices, which is what the editor shows. You don't have to touch anything in the editor. Collisions are still built from the original planes, so clipnodes don't go up.

Leave it on. Turning it off is only useful to compare with the old behavior.
Cuántas unidades tiene que separarse el:
How many units the editor's solid has to differ from the planes' solid for the brush to be rebuilt.

WHAT CHANGES: most deformed brushes differ by a few hundredths, which opens no visible slit. Rebuilding them anyway adds faces: on ze_elysium, rebuilding the 1081 candidates raised the faces each leaf sees by 17%; with 0.2, 48 are rebuilt, it costs 2% and zpa_house's slits stay closed.

Lower it only if you still see a thin slit in the game.
Los sólidos deformados pueden dejar cara: Deformed solids can leave invisible faces or slits in the game
construye el árbol, fusiona coplanares y: builds the tree, merges coplanar faces and subdivides faces
Tamaño máximo de una cara antes de parti: Maximum size of a face before it gets split. 240 is NOT a conservative number: it's the ceiling MAX_SURFACE_EXTENT imposes. If you raise it, the map stops loading in the software renderer and in HLDS. Lowering it creates more faces and lowers FPS. Leave it at 240.
Tamaño máximo, en unidades, de un nodo d:
Maximum size, in units, of a BSP tree node before it gets split.

WHAT CHANGES: smaller produces more nodes and leaves, which gives a finer PVS (VIS can cull better) but also more faces, a bigger BSP and a slower VIS. Bigger does the opposite: it compiles sooner and the PVS gets coarser.

1024 is the proven balance. Lowering it to 512 sometimes helps in very open maps, but measure it with r_speeds before calling it good: it's just as easy to make FPS worse.
Activa -lmoptimize. Reordena las caras p: Turns on -lmoptimize. Reorders the faces to waste less space on the lightmap pages. Can reduce the pages used without changing the geometry or the lighting quality.
Activa -gridsubdivide. El motor acepta u:
Turns on -gridsubdivide. The engine accepts a face as long as it touches 16 lightmap cells or fewer. The classic rule doesn't count cells: it cuts every 224 units and lets up to 240 through, so a 256 wall aligned to the grid comes out split into 224 + 32.

With this option BSP counts cells the same way the engine does and only cuts when the face goes over 16. The test maps ended up with between 3 % and 20 % fewer faces, without changing the geometry or the lighting: less wpoly and a slightly faster RAD.

BSP counts again when welding vertices and before writing the file; if a face doesn't fit, the compile stops with an error instead of leaving a map that won't load. Ignores the Subdivide value. Test the map in the game before publishing it.
no los uses para un compilado final: don't use them for a final compile
Corta BSP en cuanto termina de buscar le: Stops BSP as soon as it finishes looking for leaks. Tells you in seconds whether the map is sealed, but doesn't produce a playable map.
Activa -allleaks. Si el mapa está abiert: Turns on -allleaks. If the map is open, BSP keeps surveying and marks every hole it finds instead of stopping at the first. Useful to fix several leaks in a single pass.
Saltea el arreglo de t-junctions. Más rá: Skips the t-junction fix. Faster, but you'll see light cracks between faces. For testing only.
No genera la geometría de colisión. El m: Doesn't generate the collision geometry. The map loads but the player walks through walls. Only for looking at geometry.
calcula qué se ve desde dónde: define lo: works out what is visible from where: sets the map's FPS
El PVS que calcula VIS decide cuánto le: The PVS VIS computes decides how much the map asks of the engine every frame. The tighter it is, the less wpoly and the more FPS.
Recorta la visibilidad más allá de N uni: Cuts visibility beyond N units. Can help in huge open maps, but misused it produces geometry that pops in. 0 turns it off.
la iluminación: ~95% del tiempo de compi: the lighting: ~95% of the compile time
RAD no cambia la geometría que dibuja el: RAD doesn't change the geometry the engine draws: raising the light quality costs compile time, not in-game FPS.
Cuántos rayos lanza cada muestra hacia e: How many rays each sample casts toward the sky: level 4 = 258 rays, 5 = 1026, 6 = 4098, 7 = 16386. Measured, this loop is 96% of all of RAD's rays. Level 6 uses 4x fewer rays than 7 with a maximum difference of 1/255 per luxel, that is, invisible. That's why this fork's default is 6 and not 7.
Ilumina cada punto con todo el domo del:
Lights each point with the whole sky dome instead of a single direction.

WHAT CHANGES: with this, shadow edges outdoors are gradual, like in real life, and shaded areas get some bluish light from the sky. Without it the sun is a single direction and shadows come out hard and sharp-edged, with an old-map look.

Turning it off forces the sky level to 4 (258 rays) and speeds things up quite a bit, but the visual difference outdoors is obvious.
Toma 9 muestras de luz por cada luxel en:
Takes 9 light samples per luxel instead of 1, and averages them.

WHAT CHANGES: it's RAD's most visible quality improvement. Without it shadow edges come out stair-stepped, with the typical 16-unit lightmap jaggies; with it they're smooth. Badly computed light spots in corners and sloped surfaces also go away.

It costs compile time and ZERO in-game FPS: the resulting lightmap is exactly the same size.
Cuántas veces se le permite rebotar a la:
How many times light is allowed to bounce before it's considered spent.

WHAT CHANGES: with 0 there's only direct light, so everything a lamp doesn't see stays black. Each bounce spreads light from lit surfaces to the ones that aren't, and also tints them: a lit red floor will tint the wall next to it red. The first bounces change a lot; from ~12 on the contribution is so small it's practically indistinguishable.

It costs time, not FPS. 12 is what -extra applies in this fork.
Modo borrador de la iluminación.\n\nQUÉ:
Draft mode for the lighting.

WHAT CHANGES: lowers the sampling quality and simplifies the bounce calculation. The result is good for checking that the lights are where they belong and that nothing was left dark, but gradients come out dirty and shadows imprecise.

Useful while you build; never for the version you publish.
Tamaño, en unidades, de los parches en q:
Size, in units, of the patches RAD splits surfaces into to spread bounced light.

WHAT CHANGES: each patch emits and receives light as one unit. Smaller gives more detailed indirect light (gradients on big walls stop looking blocky), but the cost grows fast: the work goes with the square of the number of patches, so halving it can quadruple the time and the RAM.

64 is the default. If a big wall looks 'blotchy', try 48 or 32 before touching anything else.
Lo mismo que chop, pero para las superfi:
Same as chop, but for the surfaces that EMIT light: the texlights defined in lights.rad.

WHAT CHANGES: controls how much detail goes into the light coming out of a glowing sign or a fluorescent tube. Smaller makes the source's shape show in the light it casts, instead of behaving like a diffuse blob.

It's lower than chop (32 against 64) because texlights tend to be small and their shape does matter.
Ángulo máximo, en grados, para que dos c:
Maximum angle, in degrees, for two neighboring faces to be lit as if they were one continuous curved surface.

WHAT CHANGES: if the angle between two faces is below this value, RAD blends their normals and the light crosses from one to the other with no seam. Above it, it leaves a sharp edge.

Raising it smooths terrain and arches made of many faces. Overdoing it makes corners that should have a clear edge look rounded and soft. 50 degrees works for almost everything; 70 for very faceted terrain.
Activa el backend Vulkan de RAD para el:
Turns on RAD's Vulkan backend for the direct gather and the compatible transfers. If a phase or entity isn't supported, or there's no Vulkan driver, RAD reports why and falls back to the CPU.

HOW MUCH IT GAINS: depends on how many lights the map has. On ze_elysium, with 1561 direct lights, RAD went from 88 to 49 seconds on a GTX 1060. On maps with few lights the automatic selection keeps that phase on the CPU.

WHAT CHANGES: the GPU computes in float; compared to the CPU, less than 1% of the luxels change, by 3/255 at most. Turn it off if you need the .bsp identical to the CPU's.
RAD mide cada fase antes de abrir Vulkan: RAD measures each phase before opening Vulkan. Uses the CPU for small jobs, where copying the data costs more than computing it, and the GPU above the threshold.
Permite que Vulkan calcule las luces dir: Lets Vulkan compute the compatible direct lights. Unsupported entities or models fall back to the CPU without changing the result.
Permite que Vulkan calcule los factores: Lets Vulkan compute the patch-to-patch factors of the Sparse matrix. The bounces then use those same factors through the reference path.
Índice del dispositivo Vulkan que RAD de: Index of the Vulkan device RAD should use. -1 picks automatically; use a number only if you have several GPUs and know the index RAD prints.
Cómo guarda RAD la visibilidad entre par: How RAD stores the visibility between patches. It's a memory and speed decision, not a quality one: all four give the same light.
Baja el umbral de recorte de luz de 255:
Lowers the light clipping threshold from 255 to 188.

WHAT CHANGES: caps very bright areas earlier to keep the behavior expected by engines older than the 25th anniversary. It's on to keep ReSDHLT's historical default.

Not every client and fork renders the limit the same way. Before publishing, compare a bright area with your community's real client and server; turn it off if your confirmed target is the new engine.
Hace que RAD ignore la clave zhlt_studio:
Makes RAD ignore the entities' zhlt_studioshadow key.

WHAT CHANGES: that key lets a model (a tree, a fence, a statue) cast a real shadow on the map, tracing its mesh triangle by triangle. With this option models stop casting shadows: light goes through them as if they weren't there.

It only matters if your map uses that key. When it does, tracing the mesh is expensive, so turning this on speeds up test compiles quite a bit. For the final version leave it off.
Hace que todo modelo .mdl puesto como en:
Makes every .mdl placed as an entity (cycler_sprite and the like) cast a shadow, without setting zhlt_studioshadow on each one.

WHAT CHANGES: trees, crates and statues darken the floor and walls like a solid. Transparent or additive models (rendermode) are left out, and a single one is excluded with zhlt_studioshadow 0.

The .mdl files are looked up in the game folder, one level above maps\. Tracing the meshes is expensive: with many models, the compile takes longer.
Dejar que el modelo tape su luz: Let the model block its own light
Desactiva la protección del texel con el:
Turns off the protection of the texel the game lights each model with.

WHAT CHANGES: the game lights a whole model with a single lightmap texel, the one under it. If the model casts a shadow over that texel, it shows up black. By default RAD leaves that texel without the model's own shadow: the model gets the light of the spot and a slightly brighter patch remains right under it (about 5x5 texels, 3x3 with -extra).

Turn it on only if that patch is more noticeable than the dark model.
Imprime al final en qué gasta RAD el tie: Prints at the end what RAD spends its time on, with call counts. Useful to understand a slow compile, not for normal use.
todo apagado por defecto; sin tocarlo el: all off by default; untouched, the map comes out the same
Oscurece la luz en rincones, bajo repisa:
Darkens the light in corners, under ledges and next to objects, where in real life less surrounding light gets in. Each light sample casts rays over a hemisphere and is darkened by how many hit nearby geometry.

WHICH MODE TO USE: if your map is lit with light, light_spot and light_environment, 'direct light only'. If it's lit with texlights, 'all light': the other mode doesn't touch texlight light and would barely show.

It costs compile time and zero FPS.
Hasta cuántas unidades busca geometría c: How many units each ray looks for geometry. More reach darkens wider areas around each object; little reach marks only the corners.
Cuánto oscurece la oclusión: 1 es el efe: How much the occlusion darkens: 1 is the full effect, 0 does nothing. Lower it if the corners come out too black.
Cómo pesa la distancia del choque. 1 es: How the hit distance is weighted. 1 is linear. Higher keeps only the darkening hugging the geometry; lower spreads it out.
1 = 6 rayos, 2 = 18, 3 = 66, 4 = 258. Má: 1 = 6 rays, 2 = 18, 3 = 66, 4 = 258. More rays give smoother occlusion and cost more time. 3 is enough for almost everything.
Salta los rayos que casi no aportan (los: Skips the rays that barely contribute (the very grazing ones). Saves time with no visible change. 0 traces them all.
Hacia qué color tiñe la oclusión. Negro: What color the occlusion tints toward. Black is the norm; a cool or warm dark tone can give a map character.
Cuántos rayos de sombra por eje traza ca:
How many shadow rays per axis each sample traces toward each light: 1 is one ray (hard shadow, the usual), 3 is 9 rays spread over the size of a lightmap texel.

WHAT CHANGES: shadow edges go from a staircase of texels to a short gradient. Affects light, light_spot and light_environment; texlights already give soft shadows.

COST: on zm_eichen_v2, 3 took RAD from 2.5 to 3.6 s. Computes direct light on the CPU even if you use the GPU.
{rays} rayos de sombra por muestra y luz: {rays} shadow rays per sample and light. 3 is the useful value; more is barely noticeable and costs more
RAD suaviza cada luxel promediándolo con:
RAD smooths each luxel by averaging it with its neighbors. At the edge of a thin shadow or at the foot of a wall, those lit neighbors bring in light where there shouldn't be any.

WHAT CHANGES: a neighbor brighter than the luxel weighs less in the average, down to 1 - N of its weight. 0 turns it off, 0.5 is a good starting point, 1 lets no brighter neighbor in.

Acts on the direct light of light, light_spot and light_environment. A map lit almost only with texlights doesn't change.
busca agujeros, zonas caras en FPS y car: looks for holes, FPS-heavy areas and faces drawn for nothing
Vacío analiza el .bsp que dejó la última: Empty analyzes the .bsp left by this project's last compile. Pick another to check any map, even one you didn't compile yourself.
Todavía no hay un .bsp compilado para es: There is no compiled .bsp for this project yet
Lanza rayos por el mapa compilado. Donde:
Casts rays through the compiled map. Where one goes into a wall and no drawn face covers it, the player would see through: it's the invisible-faces problem of deformed brushes.

If the project's .map is this .bsp's, the rays aim at every visible face of the .map, so none slips through.
Más rayos revisan más superficie y tarda: More rays check more surface and take longer. 20000 is enough for a normal map; raise it for huge maps.
Cuenta, para cada hoja del mapa, cuántas: Counts, for each leaf of the map, how many world faces the PVS sends to the engine. That is what wpoly tracks and what lowers FPS. Lists the worst areas so you know where to place a HINT or break a line of sight.
Hojas más cerca que esto se juntan en un: Leaves closer than this are joined into a single area in the list.
Caras que se dibujan y se iluminan sin q:
Faces that are drawn and lit with nobody able to see them: world walls fully covered by a fixed func_wall, and entity faces buried inside walls. NULL or func_detail gets rid of them.

A func_illusionary doesn't count: it isn't solid, and a player can step into a bush and see the floor below.
Revisa que cada cara sea plana, convexa: Checks that every face is flat, convex and without repeated vertices, and counts the pairs of faces that could still be merged. An error here is the compiler's, not yours.
Corre el análisis solo cada vez que una: Runs the analysis by itself every time a compile ends well. Takes a few seconds and reports in this tab.

RAD elige solo. Con la GPU activada usa:
RAD picks on its own. With the GPU on it uses sparse, because the GPU only computes the transfers of that matrix and gains more that way. Without the GPU it uses the normal matrix if it fits in 512 MB, and sparse otherwise.

The normal one answers each query with a bit instead of a search: on ze_elysium it cut MakeScales from 14 to 3.4 s on the CPU. With 43,000 patches it takes 112 MB. On huge maps it switches to sparse by itself, so it does not run out of memory.

Does NOT change the resulting lighting.
Guarda en memoria, sin comprimir, qué pa:
Keeps in memory, uncompressed, which light patch sees which other one. It is the fastest of the three, but its RAM use grows with the square of the patch count: on a large map with a low -chop it can ask for several GB and fail for lack of memory.

Does NOT change the resulting lighting, only how it is computed.
Guarda esa misma información comprimida::
Keeps that same information compressed: only the pairs that actually see each other. Uses much less RAM at the cost of CPU: each query is a search. Automatic picks it on its own when the normal one does not fit.

Does NOT change the resulting lighting.
No construye ninguna matriz: recalcula l:
Builds no matrix at all: it recomputes visibility every time it needs it. RAM stops being a problem, but it is quite a bit slower. Only makes sense when the other two run out of memory.

Does NOT change the resulting lighting.
Sin oclusión ambiental. RAD escribe lo m: No ambient occlusion. RAD writes the same as always.
La AO de seedee/SDHLT: oscurece la luz d: seedee/SDHLT's AO: darkens the light from light, light_spot and light_environment in corners and next to objects. It does not touch texlight light, so a map lit with texlights barely changes.
La misma oclusión aplicada a toda la luz: The same occlusion applied to all the light at the point, texlights and bounces included. This is the one that shows on maps lit with texlights. On ze_elysium it darkened 27% of the faces for 4% more RAD time.
Cálculo aproximado de visibilidad. Compi: Approximate visibility. Compiles in seconds, but the PVS is too loose: the engine draws things that cannot actually be seen and FPS drop. Only to check that the map loads.
Cálculo completo estándar. Suficiente mi: Standard full computation. Enough while you build the map.
El PVS más ajustado que las herramientas: The tightest PVS the tools can compute. Takes longer to compile and produces FEWER wpoly in game, which means more FPS. Always use it for the version you release.
Lo más rápido posible, para comprobar qu: As fast as possible, to check that the map loads and has no leaks. The lighting looks ugly and FPS are worse than the real ones: do not judge the map by this.
El que conviene usar casi siempre. Calid: The one to use almost always. Full quality with this fork's measured improvements already applied. It is also the default on startup.
Para la versión que publicas. Igual que: For the version you release. Same as Recommended but with sky sampling at maximum (-skylevel 7). Costs ~1.65x more RAD time for a difference you cannot see: it only makes sense if you need to reproduce the original SDHLT output exactly.
Este fork arregló dos bugs por los que l: This fork fixed two bugs that made the tools use a single thread: always on Linux, and on Windows with CPUs of more than 32 logical threads. Measured, using every core gave 1.68x on a 2-core machine; with 8 the difference is much bigger. Do not enter a number by hand unless you want to leave CPU free for something else.
El flag cambia el limiter de luz para co: The flag changes the light limiter for compatibility with engines older than the 25th anniversary. It stays on as the historical default, but do not assume one setting works for every fork: test the brightest areas with the actual client and server you will release on.
VIS en 'full' para lo que publicas: VIS on 'full' for what you release
VIS es lo único que decide cuánto le pid: VIS is the only thing that decides how much the map asks of the engine each frame. 'full' takes longer to compile and gives fewer wpoly in game. Compile with 'fast' while you build if you like, but never release a map with fast VIS.
El límite de 240 no es un número conserv: The 240 limit is not a conservative number: it is the ceiling MAX_SURFACE_EXTENT imposes. Raise it and the map stops loading in the software renderer and on HLDS. Lowering it makes more faces and lowers FPS. Leave it at 240.
Los FPS los baja el mapper, no el compil: FPS are lowered by the mapper, not the compiler
La fusión de caras del BSP ya elimina en: The BSP's face merging already removes 19% to 46% of the faces (measured on three maps) and VIS's PVS is already nearly exact. What moves the needle is NULL on everything that cannot be seen, and SOLIDHINT/BEVELHINT on terrain and stairs. See docs/FPS_Y_TOOL_TEXTURES.md.
RAD no cambia la geometría que dibuja el: RAD does not change the geometry the engine draws, so -extra and more bounces cost compile time and some BSP size, but zero FPS in game. This is where you can be generous.
Mira el chart cuando compiles en serio: Watch the chart when you compile for real
Con 'chart' activado las herramientas im: With 'chart' on, the tools print how much of each engine limit you are using. It is how you find out you are heading for a limit before you hit it.
